title: AgentDrift: A Step-Labeled Benchmark of Injection-Hijacked LLM Agent Trajectories

report.one_sentence: AgentDrift addresses the absence of step-level labeled data for indirect prompt injection in LLM agents by releasing 12,536 synthetic tool-call trajectories (71,024 steps) in which every step is labeled benign, injection point, hijacked, or failed injection, and demonstrates with a surface-feature logistic regression that only 55.4% of attacks (and only 8.2% of partial hijacks) can be detected without sequence modeling.
report.problem: Existing indirect-prompt-injection benchmarks measure attack success rates against live agents and guard models judge whole traces, but no public corpus labels, step by step, where an injection enters a trajectory and which steps it corrupts, nor distinguishes resisted attacks from successful ones and from legitimate-but-suspicious content.
report.mechanism: This is a benchmark dataset, not a detection method. A single open model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, quantized) generates complete tool-call trajectories across five domains under category-specific protocols in which the label structure is specified at generation time and enforced by a closed-vocabulary structural validator implementing a regular label grammar (benign, full/partial/delayed hijack, failed attack, hard negative). Accepted trajectories are screened by an LLM judge (shown to be unreliable) and audited by hand on 1,200 trajectories. The dataset replaces trace-level or success-rate evaluation with per-step detection, localization, and attempt-versus-success tasks, with per-trajectory world context enabling world-grounded external-recipient features.

evidence.claim: The corpus contains 12,536 trajectories and 71,024 step labels across four categories and five domains, with all labels conforming to a stated regular grammar.
evidence.result: 12,536 trajectories; 71,024 steps; 4,000 benign / 5,536 attacked / 1,500 failed-attack / 1,500 hard-negative; 100% positional grammar adherence
evidence.baseline: Prior resources (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, TraceSafe, StepShield, etc.) lack the combination of per-step injection labels, a resisted class, and hard negatives (Table I)
evidence.conditions: Synthetic data from a single generator model; labels are protocol-specified, not independent human gold annotations
evidence.source_excerpt: We present AgentDrift, a benchmark of 12,536 synthetic tool-call trajectories over five agent domains in which every one of the 71,024 steps carries one of four labels: benign, injection point, hijacked, or failed injection.

evidence.claim: A surface-feature logistic regression baseline recovers only 55.4% of attacks, establishing that the benchmark cannot be solved without sequence modeling.
evidence.result: Precision 0.778, recall 0.554, F1 0.647, AUROC 0.734; recall 88.0% full hijack, 8.2% partial hijack, 23.1% delayed execution; failed attacks flagged at 0.187 vs 0.105 benign
evidence.baseline: Six-dimensional hand-crafted feature vector with logistic regression (the paper's own baseline, not an external method)
evidence.conditions: Evaluated once on the released 1,881-trajectory test split; baseline has access to world-grounded external-recipient features

evidence.claim: World-identity leakage lets a trivial lookup predictor reach 86.1% binary accuracy on the default split, so uncontrolled results on this corpus are not evidence of injection detection.
evidence.result: 86.1% binary accuracy overall (93.3%–98.2% in four domains) vs 55.8% majority-class rate; 47.7% in email
evidence.conditions: Lookup of identical world object in training split; caused by concurrent SLURM jobs creating separate world pools per category in four domains
evidence.source_excerpt: The predictor reaches 86.1% binary accuracy on the test split against a 55.8% majority-class rate, and between 93.3% and 98.2% in banking, web, coding, and medical

evidence.claim: An LLM judge is an unreliable verifier of security labels: it rejected 99.6% of hard negatives as malicious, fooled by the surface cues the class exists to penalize.
evidence.result: Screening pass rates: benign 89.6%, full hijack 3.6%, delayed execution 1.4%, hard negatives 0.4%; manual audit found 99.6% label correctness on 1,200 trajectories
evidence.baseline: Programmatic grammar checks (100% adherence) and 1,200-trajectory manual audit (99.6% correct)
evidence.conditions: Same model (Llama-3.3-70B) at temperature 0.1 with category-specific checklists; screening verdicts not used to filter the release
evidence.source_excerpt: the reviewer marked 1,494 of 1,500 as BAD because their observations “contain suspicious content” and “should be labeled as malicious”; that is, it was fooled by exactly the surface cues that the class exists to penalize

evidence.claim: The corpus has measurable template concentration and attack-goal-family collapse that enable memorization shortcuts.
evidence.result: 28.9% of injected observations name an ext-audit.com address; ~75% of hard negatives mention $5,000, an in-domain audit@ address, or a transfer; external-recipient fraction is 0.47–0.57 across all six attack-goal families
evidence.conditions: 4-gram analysis over the released corpus; family tags released as metadata only, not certified classification targets

minimum_test: Download the released corpus (CC BY 4.0, GitHub) and verify the counts and grammar claims directly: 12,536 trajectories, per-category label strings matching the stated regular languages, and the 70/15/15 split.

Reproduce the world-identity lookup check (Table XI) on the test split; if a world-lookup predictor does not reach ~86% binary accuracy on your copy, the leakage claim fails; if it does, apply world anonymization or a world-held-out split before any further evaluation.

Re-implement the six-feature logistic regression baseline (specified in Section IX-A, reproducible 'with a few lines of code') and confirm it recovers ~55% of attacks overall but under 25% on partial hijacks and delayed executions; if simple features solve those patterns, the paper's core difficulty claim fails.

Train a small sequence model (e.g., a short transformer or BiLSTM over the documented step linearization) on CPU or a single small GPU under the world-anonymized protocol; if it does not beat the surface baseline on partial-hijack and delayed-execution recall, the claimed need for sequence modeling is not demonstrated on your workload.
Spot-audit a random sample of attacked and hard-negative trajectories by hand against the category definitions to check whether the 99.6% label-correctness claim holds for your use case.
main_risks: All 12,536 trajectories come from a single generator model, so a detector may learn the generator's stylistic fingerprint rather than injection semantics; transfer to production agent traces is untested.
World-identity leakage in four domains means results on the default split without anonymization or world-held-out splitting are not evidence of injection detection.
Template concentration (28.9% of injections naming one fictitious domain; ~75% of hard negatives sharing three motifs) permits memorization unless target domains and amounts are masked at test time.
Injections almost always fall at step 2 or 3 under fixed positional templates, enabling positional-prior shortcuts.
Labels are protocol-specified and structurally validated rather than independently human-annotated; the 99.6% correctness figure is an estimate from a 1,200-trajectory sample.
Short trajectories (3–11 steps), single agents, and no real agent traffic limit applicability to long-horizon or multi-agent settings.
unanswered_questions: Does a sequence-aware detector trained on AgentDrift actually outperform the surface baseline under the world-anonymized and world-held-out protocols, and by how much on partial hijack and delayed execution?
Does training on this synthetic distribution transfer to real agent traces or to trajectories from other generators?
What inter-annotator agreement would human labeling of the injection index and hijacked span yield (listed as future work)?
Are the released GitHub artifacts (data files, tool pools, loader) complete and consistent with the paper's reported counts?
What compute budget is needed to train a competitive sequence model on the corpus (not reported; only the trivial baseline is evaluated)?

technical_core.summary: The technical core is the evaluation protocol, not a new formula.
